demand_source.title: Health checks
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw's own guide presents the health commands, probe endpoints and uptime monitoring as the operator's way to verify that the Gateway and its channels work.

edits.description: Host-side, read-only checks that text Tony only when something is broken or has changed: an expired or expiring sign-in, a failed channel probe, a plugin that did not load, a new audit finding, the firewall or FileVault off, a new listening port, automatic macOS update checks switched off. The monthly run also carries the operator's standing checklist: spend caps, backups, a review of standing approvals and key rotation.
edits.how: Daily: a command automation runs `openclaw health --json`, `channels status --probe`, `models status --check` and, once installed, `gog auth list --check`, reading each entry and not exit codes. After every update and monthly: a happy-deploy script works through the bundled healthcheck checklist host-side (`openclaw security audit --deep` with `--json`, `gateway status --deep`, `doctor --lint`, then listening ports, firewall, FileVault, Time Machine and the software-update schedule), compares findings with the previous run and prints `NO_REPLY` when nothing changed. Most of these commands already exist on demand in happy-inspect (`audit-json`, `status`, `doctor`, `channel`), and the findings accepted at M1 are already listed in happy-config under baseline/accepted-findings.md, so the new work is the schedule, the comparison and the text; that accepted list is mirrored into `security.audit.suppressions`, or the script filters on it, so known findings stay quiet. Monthly checklist lines: every new agent or key has its own capped OpenAI project and a term in the daily cost alert; a quarterly restore drill into a scratch folder; each new store is inside the nightly archive. The roadmap's two other standing lines ride on the same monthly run: review the standing approvals, and rotate keys each quarter.
caveats: The five-minute dead-man probe that already runs reads the Gateway's readiness endpoint, which the docs say fails when a configured channel account fails its readiness check, and the roadmap's M1 Grafana alerts cover 'gateway down' and 'iMessage unhealthy'. So the new daily work is expiring sign-ins and model credentials and plugins that failed to load; the live channel probe is a second opinion and not a new alert. Do not build the same alert twice.
The Google half of the daily check waits until the gog command-line tool is installed.
The roadmap already says to re-run the audit after each update; this only makes it automatic and change-based.
Plain doctor can migrate state, so scheduled checks use the lint form, and the audit's fix flag is never used in a scheduled job.

The deep audit probes the live Gateway and loads plugin security collectors, so it runs while the Gateway is up. On this install it has only been run on demand, from the admin session through happy-inspect and from happy's own session (M0 and M1 sign-offs), where its live probe returns a missing-scope warning that is on the accepted list; a run from the scheduler is untested.

demand_source.title: Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems (OpenAI), section 4.4 Legibility of Agent Activity
demand_source.supports: OpenAI's guidance says it may be particularly important that whoever deploys an agent gives the user a ledger of the actions it took, as a lighter way than approvals to let people see what was done for them.

edits.how: Actions (G006): `openclaw audit --kind tool_action` gives tool names and outcomes, never arguments, so the target of each action comes from an in-house record (an `after_tool_call` hook, or the journal rows the write tools keep for undo, CRT-01) in one table in the household store (F031). Approvals are not in those tool-action rows and the approvals command lists only pending requests; OpenClaw shows an approval's outcome only when one run is inspected at a time (`openclaw audit --run <id> --explain`), so for a weekly count the 'approvals given' line comes from the same table: the in-house hook that asks for a yes writes a row from its `onResolution` callback, which receives allow-once, allow-always, deny, timeout or cancelled. A command automation renders the Sunday text from that table with no model; a small read tool that returns only the asker's own rows answers on request. Memory (F085): the week's saves come from the same per-write record, or from a weekly isolated automation per adult limited to `memory_search` and `memory_get`. Forgetting (F085, operator runbook): `openclaw memory forget --agent <id> --session <id-or-key> --dry-run`, read the report, repeat without `--dry-run`, then hand-delete the lines listed under `curatedWrites`.

demand_source.title: Get to know your Emergency Kit (1Password Support)
demand_source.supports: A shipping password manager tells customers to print a recovery sheet, keep it somewhere safe and give a copy to someone they trust, such as a spouse, so access survives when the owner is unavailable.

edits.how: No new software. The card lists: (1) how to tell: no reply within a few minutes; also add Jordan as a second recipient of the existing dead-man alert. (2) The pause phrase (G005) and that it is always safe to use. (3) After a power cut the Mac waits at the FileVault screen: type the password from the envelope at the Mac, then log in the happy user so Messages runs. The gateway and its helpers are launch agents in the happy user's login session (M0 sign-off), so they start by themselves once happy is logged in and not before. Apple's remote unlock over SSH needs Apple silicon, macOS 26, Remote Login on and a network connection, and the roadmap notes it works from the home network only, so it does not help someone who is away. (4) The commands that may be needed if Happy is still silent: logged in as happy, 'openclaw gateway status' and 'openclaw gateway restart' (the docs say not to chain stop and start). The house scripts are the operator's repair tools and go with the second envelope: from Tony's admin account 'happy-inspect ready' is a read-only check, while 'happy-deploy --restart' also restarts (ready within about ten seconds at M0) but first applies whatever config is staged, so it is not the card's restart step. (5) Who to call. The envelope holds what the card needs and where the config repo and backups are. Separately, set a Legacy Contact on the Apple Accounts involved so the account behind Happy's iMessage identity can be recovered in the worst case; Apple's legacy access leaves out Keychain passwords, so the API keys still depend on the nightly backup (its checklist lines are now in G008). Rehearse once: Tony leaves the house, Jordan restarts the Mac and brings Happy back from the card. Least privilege, from review: the happy user holds a secure token on this Mac (read with sysadminctl in this review), and Apple's FileVault management page says unlocking needs a secure token and, on Apple silicon, volume ownership. If happy's password unlocks the disk at the startup screen, that one step also logs happy in, which is all a power cut needs. The first envelope then holds only happy's password and the admin credential goes in a second envelope for repairs. Confirm this at the rehearsal before relying on it.

demand_source.title: Computer use
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw's computer-use guide tells an operator who does not want screen control to put the command on the Gateway deny list, and says a denied command is withheld and logged.

edits.description: Make 'no agent can drive, run commands on or view any Mac, or pull data from a paired phone' an explicit Gateway setting instead of a side effect of no app being installed, and write down the three ways to switch computer control off. No Mac or phone is paired as a node today (the two Control UI entries on Tony's iPhone are operator consoles, not nodes), so the family sees no change; it is the gate the iPhone app (OCL-01) and the screen-control pilot (MAC-02) must pass first.
edits.how: Add `computer.act` to `gateway.nodes.commands.deny` in happy-config, and while no Mac node is wanted also every desktop host command the docs list as arriving with a Mac pairing: `system.run`, `system.run.prepare`, `system.which`, `browser.proxy`, `browser.proxy.upload.v1`, `mcp.tools.call.v1`, `screen.snapshot` and `desktop.stream`. A deny entry always wins over platform defaults and allow entries, matches exact command names, withholds the command (for `computer.act`, together with the node's `computer` capability) and is logged. The list is Gateway-wide, so the same change carries the phone ceiling for the iPhone app entry (OCL-01): deny the iOS default data commands (`location.get`, `contacts.search`, `calendar.events`, `reminders.list`, `photos.latest`, `motion.activity`, `motion.pedometer`) and the four push-to-talk commands (`talk.ptt.start`, `talk.ptt.stop`, `talk.ptt.cancel`, `talk.ptt.once`), which any node that advertises talk otherwise gets by default and which come off the list only when Talk (VOX-01) is set up; keep the opt-in commands (`camera.snap`, `camera.clip`, `screen.record`, `health.summary`, `contacts.add`, `calendar.add`, `reminders.add`) out of `gateway.nodes.commands.allow`, and set `gateway.nodes.pluginTools.enabled: false` so a paired device cannot publish tools to agents. Keep `computer` absent from every agent's tool lists; the per-person agents already deny `group:nodes`, which contains it, and the inbox agent denies every tool. Pairing is already manual-only in the config repo since M0 (`gateway.nodes.pairing.autoApproveLocal: false` and `sshVerify: false`; SSH-verified pairing is otherwise on by default), so keep both and do not use setup links for a Mac, since a setup link can still approve a node's first command surface automatically. The happy-inspect posture check reads only the first of the two; add `sshVerify`, the deny list and `pluginTools.enabled` to it. Leave `gateway.nodes.pairing.autoApproveCidrs` unset (it is off unless set), so no device is approved by network address alone. The deny list covers paired nodes; control of the Gateway's own desktop is a separate route that the docs say needs the `cua-computer` plugin explicitly enabled on the Gateway host, so never run `openclaw plugins enable cua-computer` on the Mac mini. For reference, the documented gate stack for screen control is: tool policy exposes `computer` to an agent; gateway command policy; device pairing and then a second, distinct approval of the node's command surface; the switch inside the Mac app; and the macOS permissions. Exec approvals gate shell commands on a node, not clicks. Off switches during a pilot: (1) put the deny line back (command-policy changes reach connected nodes under the default hybrid reload, with no restart); (2) the G005 kill file checked in the desk hook; (3) on the Mac, turn off 'Allow Computer Control' (rechecked at each invocation) or revoke Accessibility.
caveats: Without this, once OpenClaw.app is installed on any family Mac, its pairing is approved and the macOS permissions are granted, pointer and keyboard control is available to any agent later given `computer` and to any caller with operator write access, because `computer.act` is in the macOS default allowlist and the app switch defaults on.
The deny list is global, not per Mac. The per-Mac controls are the pairing approval and the switch inside the app, so a pilot that lifts a deny entry lifts it for every paired node.
`screen.record` is already off unless explicitly allowed; `screen.snapshot` and `desktop.stream` are not, once a pairing that declares them is approved.

The two-step approval (device, then command surface) is not unconditional: SSH-verified pairing and setup-code enrollment can approve a node's first surface automatically. SSH-verified pairing is already switched off in this config; setup codes remain.
The same pairing that would arm `computer.act` also brings shell execution, a browser proxy, node MCP calls and a desktop stream, which is why the deny list names those commands too.

edits.how: Clean desk (MAC-03): a macOS guest on the Mac mini built with Apple's Virtualization framework (for example the Lume CLI) and reset to a known snapshot before every run; OpenClaw.app is installed inside the guest, paired as its own node and granted Accessibility and Screen Recording there; files move only through the File Transfer plugin limited to one folder. What only the native app adds is the share sheet, the offline queue, the native inbox and Talk mode (VOX-01), for which this entry is the install and pairing step. edits.how:
1. Ceiling first, before any phone is paired: confirm the wave-A deny list (MAC-04) is deployed. It denies the iOS default data commands and the four push-to-talk commands (talk.ptt.start, talk.ptt.stop, talk.ptt.cancel, talk.ptt.once; taken off the deny list only when Talk, VOX-01, is set up), keeps the opt-in commands (camera, screen recording, Health and the contact, calendar and reminder writes) out of gateway.nodes.commands.allow and sets gateway.nodes.pluginTools.enabled: false, so a paired phone cannot publish tools to agents. 2. Install the App Store app on Tony's iPhone and pair it with a setup code from the Control UI (Nodes, Devices, Pair device) or openclaw qr over the existing Tailscale Serve URL. One code issues a node session and an operator session together; an administrator-minted code approves the device and its first declared command surface in one step, so read the approved command list afterwards and approve any later widening by hand. 3. Access level: Full access carries operator.admin, which is what lets the app review pending exec approvals in general; Limited access drops only operator.admin (write, read and approvals scopes remain) and the docs then promise approval review only for requests that explicitly target that device. The Control UI already paired on this phone holds admin scope, and approving from the Control UI passed at M1, so pairing the app Limited gives up nothing that is not already on the phone. 4. Agents: do not grant the built-in nodes tool to any agent (it is owner-only, on the sandbox default deny list, and carries approve and raw invoke actions); if a later feature needs one phone command, use a small in-house plugin tool over api.runtime.nodes.invoke with the node id and command fixed in code. Deny show_widget on

-main, or allow native reports only. 5. Uploads from the app go through the local privacy gate that now sits in the photo and PDF entry (F002, formerly F084), or are switched off with gateway.uploads.enabled: false; that switch is Gateway-wide and is not set today, so the same upload path is already open in the Control UI on Tony's phone. iMessage stays the main channel and the Control UI stays the backup approval path it already is (M1 sign-off); the native app is a nicer surface for long documents and tap approvals, a second fallback if imsg breaks after a macOS update, and the install that Talk (VOX-01) needs. Out of scope for this entry: a second adult's phone. Every setup code carries Gateway-wide operator scopes, OpenClaw says those are not isolation between people, and roadmap section 1b keeps the control plane with Tony while family members only chat. Reopening that is Tony's decision, and it would first need named operator roles (gateway.roles) bound to a verified identity and rehearsed on a test profile, because a Gateway with roles configured refuses operator connections that carry only a device or setup-code token.

who_trigger_result: A parent / asks about a public page that only shows with JavaScript, or sends a link to a long article or a captioned video / the research helper reads it logged out and the parent's own agent relays the answer with the link.

demand_source.title: Browser (OpenClaw-managed): What you get
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw documents a separate, agent-only browser whose supported uses include answering questions from a page's readable text.

edits.how: Two readers, on the research agent only. (1) The `browser` tool on the managed `openclaw` profile, with `headless: true` on that profile and `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`. Up to four switches come first: `browser.enabled` (off since M0, and possibly not needed, see below), the browser tool on research's sandbox tool allow list (it is on the sandbox default deny list), the per-agent tool allow, and a place for the browser to live. First choice is the roadmap's sandbox browser container with the LAN blocked, which has a switch of its own (`sandbox.browser.enabled`, off by default and off in today's config, to be turned on for research only); its image has to be built from a source checkout because the npm install does not include the Dockerfile. The sandbox reference says this container browser does not require the top-level `browser.enabled`, while the browser setup page says the agent tool needs it, so try it with `browser.enabled` left off first: if that works, the host's browser control service is never switched on. The fallback is the host's managed profile through `sandbox.browser.allowHostControl` and an explicit host target, which the docs say to keep off for sandboxed agents unless you trust them. (2) A host stdio MCP that wraps `summarize --extract --json` and returns extracted text from articles, and from YouTube videos and podcasts that publish captions or a transcript, without calling a model; the wrapper pins `--firecrawl off`, holds no third-party keys, sets up no transcription fallback and checks the address itself. The firewall (formerly WEB-03): an in-house plugin with `api.on("before_tool_call", handler, { matcher: ["browser"] })`, default-deny and failing closed. It rejects any `profile`, `target` or `node` other than the one assigned to the agent (a missing profile is filled in or blocked, because an omitted profile means the default one) and rejects `systemProfile`, `into`, `domains` and `dashboard`. Of the tool's 24 actions it allows only a listed read-only subset (for example status, tabs, open, navigate, focus, close, snapshot, text, screenshot). `act` and `upload` are not on that list in this build, which blocks every act kind at once: `batch`, `evaluate`, `press`, `clickCoords`, `drag`, `wait`, `resize`, `type`, `fill`, `select` and `click`. If a page later proves unreadable without scrolling, `act` comes back only for kinds on an allowlist of its own (`scrollIntoView`, `hover`), each with an eval case. The hook reads the URL from `targetUrl` first and `url` second, looks inside a nested `request` object, and blocks any call whose top-level and nested kinds differ. Unknown agent, missing field, unknown action or kind, or a parse error returns a block; the runner itself blocks the call if the handler throws or times out. Research reads the open web, so there is no site allowlist here; navigation stays http and https under the private-network block in F019 (formerly WEB-01). Not built here: the exact-hostname allowlist and the ask-a-parent-before-typing approval branch, whose only consumer is the roadmap's M6 jobs agent.
unverified: `--youtube auto` and the optional Apify token appear in the bundled skill but not on the upstream README; check `summarize --help` after install.
How often rec-portal and store pages block a headless, logged-out browser was not measured.
The hook contract was read, but the browser parameter names come from the tool's schema source and were not observed in a live hook event.
Whether `ctx.agentId` carries the sub-agent's id when research runs as a spawned session; every per-agent rule depends on it.
Whether the hook sees the browser call before the tool applies its own defaults (profile, target), so that 'must be present' can be enforced.
Whether script-rendered pages can be read with the `act` action off (no `wait`, `click` or scrolling); any kind allowed back needs its own eval case.
What summarize returns for a video without captions when no transcription engine is configured (an error or an empty result); the README does not say and the tool is not installed.

Whether the sandbox browser gives research a working `browser` tool with the top-level `browser.enabled` left false: the sandbox configuration page says it is not required, the browser setup page says the tool needs it.

evidence.title: Agent sandbox configuration: browser
evidence.supports: The sandboxed container browser has its own switch, off by default, and the page says it does not need the top-level browser switch.

evidence.title: Browser setup: Plugin control
evidence.supports: The browser setup page says the agent tool by default needs both the plugin and the top-level browser switch.
